title: Dragonfly and damselfly flight dates moved 3-6.5 days earlier per 1 C of pre-flight warmth in 11 European regions in 1990-2024; recorder-effort drift leaves the long-term advance unresolved
abstract: Question: do European Odonata flight seasons follow temperature in the same way in independent regions, how much of the 1990-2024 change does temperature explain, and how large is the recorder-effort error in opportunistic records? Data: 9.36 million dated GBIF records (daily facet counts) of 93 species in 11 regions (Netherlands, two British, two French and Swiss regions for 1990-2024; two German regions, Sweden, Finland and Spain for 2008-2024), 528 species-region series, and E-OBS v32.0e daily temperature. Method: a plan with seven hypotheses was written and hashed before any date data were downloaded; per species-region regressions of the median (P50) and early (P10) flight date on the mean temperature of the 90 days before flight and on previous-summer temperature; random-effects pooling; waterbird and all-bird placebo series in the same windows; effort weighting; a single-dataset replication; a 1990-2012 to 2013-2024 out-of-sample test. Results: P50 moved -4.69 days per C (95% CI -5.25 to -4.14), with region means from -3.0 (Sweden) to -6.5 (southern Britain); the result held with a year term (-4.58), after 2000 (-4.44), in single datasets (-5.07) and with effort weights (-3.83). Early-flying and larval-overwintering species were more sensitive (+3.2 days per C per 100 days of later flight; egg overwinterers +2.1). Region-year mean predictions for 2013-2024 had r = 0.88 and skill 0.78 against the 1990-2012 mean, but species-year skill was only 0.13 (-0.05 to 0.28), so the planned out-of-sample rule failed. Two earlier claims did not repeat: P10 was not more sensitive than P50 (difference +0.40, 0.09 to 0.71), and a warm previous summer did not delay flight (+0.10, -0.37 to 0.57). Median dates advanced 2.1 days per decade in the long-series regions, and temperature predicted 37-97% of this. But waterbird placebo records in the same windows also moved earlier by 1.7-6.2 days per decade, and effort-weighted trends were near zero in four regions. Conclusion: the interannual temperature response is strong and general; the long-term advance from opportunistic records is not identified without a better effort measure. Limitations: opportunistic records, regional temperature means, bird-based effort calendar, literature-coded overwintering stages, short series in five regions.

citations.reason: Temperature explained most of the advance of one-brood British butterflies; we find a similar strong interannual response in Odonata.
